title: Structural concrete that stores building-relevant energy

concept.text: The innovation is concrete that performs two useful jobs in the same material: carrying structural loads and storing electrical energy that a building can later use. Its defining achievement would be enough usable storage within a realistic building concrete volume to provide a meaningful electrical service while retaining the material’s structural function. Concrete surrounding a conventional battery pack would not establish this capability; the structural material itself must participate in storage.

The supplied research describes cement-based structural supercapacitors as a possible route. The target, however, extends beyond showing that a small specimen can store charge and has measurable compressive strength. A useful member must combine structural performance, charge storage and delivery, electrical connections, and practical construction. Separate strength and electrical measurements do not establish that a member can repeatedly charge and discharge while carrying representative loads. These are scope distinctions synthesized from the research and review.

significance.text: If successful, the innovation would turn some material already needed to support buildings into distributed electrical storage. A wall or floor could contribute both structural capacity and usable energy capacity, potentially reducing the need to allocate separate space to storage equipment. The civil-engineering breakthrough would be a practical, code-usable structural material with an additional energy function, even if its electrochemistry draws on advances in materials science and electrical engineering. This is a conditional impact assessment, not a claim that such a product has been achieved.

Building-scale storage could, conditionally, shift electricity use across time or support selected loads during interruptions. Participation in grid services would require more than stored energy: suitable charging and discharging power, controls, electrical protection, connections, and deployment at useful scale would also be necessary. The amount of energy stored alone cannot establish backup duration, peak-load support, or grid value. These are downstream possibilities and integration requirements inferred from the proposed capability.

The impact would remain application-specific. Demonstrating one structural wall or floor panel would not establish suitability for frames, pavements, or every exposure and loading condition. Nor would the dual function automatically establish lower cost, lower environmental impact, or a practical advantage over conventional storage. Those benefits would depend on the complete installation, its durability, and the amount of concrete that can actually be used for storage. These limits are part of the concept’s impact assessment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a constructible structural member that retains its required mechanical performance while repeatedly storing and returning building-relevant usable energy. The supplied reports identify candidate laboratory results, but the available evidence does not establish whether energy density, cycling under structural stress, safety, cost, or member-scale casting and precasting meet that target. These dimensions remain questions to resolve; the evidence does not justify declaring that every one has already been demonstrated inadequate.

Engineering synthesis: a practical material must reconcile the structures needed for electrical storage and conduction with those needed for strength, stiffness, and durability. Investigations would need to determine how structural loading, cracking, moisture conditions, and repeated electrical operation affect both functions together. Adequate compressive strength at one age cannot establish long-term structural durability, and successful electrical cycling without representative load cannot establish performance in a working member.

Engineering synthesis: scaling also requires dependable electrical interfaces and isolation, defined operating conditions, and a construction method that preserves performance across a full member. The counted storage volume must include a realistic allowance for regions or components that do not store energy. Cost and compatibility must be evaluated for the installed system, including connections and associated equipment. The supplied research attributes discussion of cost, compatibility, and deployment challenges to a December 2025 review, but that review’s text was not retained for verification.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies laboratory publications reporting cement-based structural supercapacitors. It describes abstract-level access, including explicitly limited access for the mortar study, but the source index contains no retained abstracts or full texts. Consequently, the numerical results and bibliographic details below are attributed reports that cannot be independently checked from the supplied evidence. This access limitation leaves their interpretation unresolved; it does not show that the results are false or that the underlying concept is invalid.

The research attributes “Cement-based structural supercapacitors with structural optimization and conductive fiber reinforcement” to Jiaxi Mao, Shenhao Ye, Suxi Wang, Jialong Lin, Dongming Yan, Shikun Chen, and Yi Liu, and lists it in Journal of Power Sources 657, article 238127, dated November 30, 2025. It reports an areal energy density of 175.36 μWh/cm² and compressive strength of 23.1 MPa at 28 days. An areal energy figure cannot establish capacity per cubic metre without the relevant device thickness and measurement boundaries. The research says thickness was absent from the retrieved abstract, but the missing retained text prevents checking that omission, the reported measurements, or whether electrical performance was measured under structural load.

A separate study, “Interconnected Conductive Networks in Cement Mortar Enable High-Performance Structural Supercapacitors,” is listed in the research as Energy Storage Materials 82, article 104630, October 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.ensm.2025.104630. The attributed results are volumetric energy density of 48.5 μWh/cm³ and compressive strength of 32.22 MPa. Author names were not expanded in the retrieved record, and the retained evidence does not permit checking the measurements or their conditions. The unit conversion is independently correct: 48.5 μWh/cm³ equals 0.0485 kWh/m³. At that density, approximately 2,062 m³ would nominally store 100 kWh, provided the density applies to the entire counted volume and survives at member scale. This arithmetic is a conditional scale illustration, not a demonstrated building capacity; 100 kWh also cannot be assumed to cover a particular building’s daily use without measuring its demand.

The research lists “Concrete: From infrastructure to structural energy storage” in Materials Today 91, pages 364–374, December 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.mattod.2025.10.016, and attributes discussion of continuing cost, compatibility, and deployment challenges to it. Its text and expanded author information are unavailable in the supplied record, so that characterization remains attributed rather than independently confirmed. The supplied evidence establishes neither a building-scale demonstration nor the absence of one elsewhere. It also provides no basis for assessing subsequent developments through November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a full structural wall or floor panel should meet a specified structural-concrete strength requirement and deliver independently metered usable energy capacity and round-trip efficiency over a stated cycle life while under representative structural loading. The report should define the loading, operating conditions, charging and discharging power, electrical measurement boundaries, and changes in structural and electrical performance over time. This is a proposed evidence package, not an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Structural panel meets strength requirements while storing energy under loading

completion_criteria.text: Proposed building-relevance threshold: demonstrate enough usable stored energy to cover a measured day of the host building’s ordinary electrical consumption, or establish member-scale usable capacity per unit volume that would provide that energy within a stated, realistically available concrete inventory. The calculation should identify which concrete can participate and account for inactive regions and necessary supporting components. A laboratory density extrapolated directly to all concrete in a building would not establish this result, and a coin-cell or thin coupon would not meet the proposed member-scale scope.
completion_criteria.label: Usable storage covers one measured day within realistic concrete inventory

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: disclose enough material, fabrication, curing, geometry, and test information for independent teams to reproduce the result, and demonstrate consistency across multiple members or batches. State the demonstrated bounds of load, environment, operating conditions, and cycle life. Finite tests would establish performance within those bounds, not universal suitability across structural applications.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduction details accompany consistent member performance and demonstrated operating bounds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical assessment: document electrical safety, durability, construction feasibility, installed cost, and the behavior of both functions when damage or degradation occurs. Meeting the panel demonstration would establish a bounded combined capability; it would not by itself establish code acceptance or readiness for routine deployment. Broader use would require evidence appropriate to the intended member, exposure, service life, and electrical installation.
completion_criteria.label: Practical assessment reports safety, feasibility, and behavior under degradation

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: CIV-01, “A primary structural binder at global cement scale without process carbon dioxide,” addresses binder production emissions, whereas CIV-10 addresses electrical storage during use. Combining them could be valuable, but neither capability implies the other. CIV-05, “Tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost,” addresses mechanical behavior and reinforcement substitution. CIV-11, “Default-cost reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior and no corrosion in ordinary exposures,” addresses reinforcement durability. CIV-10 would still need to accommodate the structural system and reinforcement selected for its application.

Roster-based comparison: CIV-04, “Repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking,” could overlap with CIV-10 where damage affects storage or electrical continuity, but restoring load capacity would not establish restoration of energy performance. CIV-07, “Load-bearing engineered living materials for ordinary structures,” shares the ambition of giving structural material additional functions, while targeting a different material capability. Neither living behavior nor self-recovery is a requirement of CIV-10.

Roster-based comparison: CIV-09, “Immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake, at life-safety cost,” concerns whole-building post-earthquake performance. Storage concrete might conditionally support selected electrical services, but stored energy cannot establish structural safety or immediate occupancy. CIV-12, “Fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost,” concerns controlled structural response. CIV-10 could potentially supply energy to an adaptive system, but storage capability and fail-safe adaptation require separate demonstrations.

Roster-based comparison: CIV-08, “Large-reservoir storage that passes sediment without giving up carryover water,” addresses retention of water-storage service while managing sediment. Its shared theme with CIV-10 is obtaining more useful service from infrastructure, but reservoir carryover storage and electrochemical energy storage have different functions and completion criteria.

Roster-based comparison: CIV-02, “Mechanics-based prediction of earthquake liquefaction and its ground consequences,” concerns predictive ground mechanics; CIV-03, “In-place conversion of ordinary ground into a specified engineering solid,” concerns ground transformation; and CIV-06, “Underground routes and spaces at surface-infrastructure cost,” concerns underground construction economics. Storage concrete could conceivably be used in infrastructure involving these concepts, but success in CIV-10 would establish none of their central capabilities.

change_log.change: Preserved CIV-10’s identity and expanded the explanation of combined structural and electrical function.
change_log.reason: The coherent innovation remains distinct from installing conventional batteries in buildings, despite unresolved supporting evidence.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical assertions of laboratory achievement and universal performance shortfalls with attributed results and specific unresolved capabilities.
change_log.reason: No retained source texts support independently verifying the results or declaring all listed performance dimensions inadequate.

change_log.change: Retained the reported strengths, energy densities, publication details, and access limitations with explicit attribution.
change_log.reason: Useful quantitative and bibliographic detail should survive consolidation without implying direct inspection or confirmation.

change_log.change: Confirmed the unit conversion and refined the scale illustration to approximately 2,062 m³ for nominally 100 kWh.
change_log.reason: The arithmetic is valid independently of source verification, but its building interpretation depends on volume boundaries, usable capacity, and successful scaling.

change_log.change: Separated independent strength and electrical measurements from cycling under representative structural load.
change_log.reason: Demonstrating each function separately does not demonstrate their reliable simultaneous operation.

change_log.change: Qualified grid benefits and extensions to frames and pavements, and removed the absolute separation of cement from the grid.
change_log.reason: Grid services require power delivery and integration, while different structural applications require their own validation.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to define usable energy, measurement boundaries, loading, available concrete volume, reproducibility, and practical limits.
change_log.reason: These details make the proposal assessable without presenting it as a consensus standard or equating strength compliance with code readiness.

change_log.change: Added distinct comparisons with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Related capabilities and possible combinations should be explained without merging concepts or implying that one breakthrough establishes another.

unresolved_issues: The supplied source index contains no retained abstracts or full texts. Author attributions, publication details, reported measurements, and the review’s characterization cannot be independently verified from these inputs.

For the Mao study, the relevant device thickness, electrical measurement boundaries, and whether testing combined electrical cycling with representative structural loading remain unknown. The claimed omission of thickness from the abstract is also unverified.
For the mortar study, the volume denominator, operating conditions, usable device capacity, and relationship between strength testing and electrical testing remain unresolved.
No supplied evidence establishes whether reported laboratory performance survives member-scale fabrication, repeated structural loading, environmental exposure, and long-term electrical operation.
The realistic storage-enabled concrete inventory, host-building demand, delivered power, efficiency, safety, installed cost, and code acceptance pathway remain unspecified.
The supplied record does not establish developments after the listed 2025 publications through November 1, 2026; it cannot support a comprehensive claim about present maturity.
